(p-70) Surah an-Nur

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A surah which We have sent down﴾, meaning: this is a surah which We have sent down. It is possible that He singled it out with this opening for two reasons:

The first: its purpose is admonition and warning, so it opens with awe, like Surat at-Tawbah.

The second: in it is an honouring of the Prophet ﷺ through the purity of his wives, so it opens with the mention of it. The word surah is a term for a noble station, and for this reason a section of the Qur'an was called a surah. The poet said:

"Did you not see that God gave you a surah, [a rank] at which every king is bewildered and trembles?"

﴿And We have made it obligatory﴾ — here there are two readings: with the light form (takhfif) and with the intensive form (tashdid).

As for whoever reads it with the light form, there are two interpretations of it:

The first: We made obligatory in it the permissibility of the lawful and the prohibition of the unlawful. This is what Mujahid said.

(p-71) The second: We determined in it the limits, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then half of what you have specified﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], meaning you determined. This is what Ikrimah said.

As for whoever reads it with the intensive form, there are two interpretations of it:

The first: its meaning is the multiplication of what was made obligatory in it of the lawful and the unlawful. This is what Ibn 'Isa said.

The second: its meaning is that We explained it. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said.

﴿And We have sent down in it clear signs﴾ — in it there are two interpretations:

The first: they are the proofs indicating His oneness and the obligation of obeying Him.

The second: they are the limits and rulings which He prescribed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator — flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾. The mention of the female fornicator was placed before the male for two reasons:

The first: fornication by her is more shameful, and because of pregnancy it is more harmful.

The second: desire in her is greater and overpowers her more.

The prescribed punishment for it was fixed at a hundred lashes for the free and the virgin, and this is the greatest of the lashing punishments, because the act of fornication is graver than the accusation of fornication. The Sunnah added to the lashing the banishment for a year after it, based on the saying of the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Take from me, God has made a way for them: for the virgin with the virgin, a hundred lashes and banishment for a year." The Iraqis prohibited banishment, limiting themselves to lashing alone, and this involves rejecting the Sunnah and the report.

The word jald (lashing) is derived from the reaching of the blow to the skin (jild). As for the married (muhsanun), their punishment is stoning by the Sunnah, either as an explanation of His saying in Surat an-Nisa': ﴿Confine them to houses until death takes them or God makes for them a way﴾ [an-Nisa': 15], according to one group; or as a beginning of legislation, according to others.

Zirr ibn Hubaysh narrated from Ubayy that in his codex, from Surat al-Ahzab, the stoning was mentioned: "If an old man and an old woman commit adultery, then stone them absolutely as a punishment from God, and God is Mighty and Wise."

(p-72) ﴿And let not pity for them take hold of you in the religion of God﴾, meaning in the obedience of God; religion is sometimes used to express obedience.

﴿If you should believe in God and the Last Day﴾, meaning: if you uphold obedience to God as one who believes in God and the Last Day does. Pity is mercy, and He did not forbid it, because God is the One who places it in hearts; He only forbade what mercy calls one to. On this there are two views:

The first: that mercy calls him to drop the prescribed punishment so that it is not carried out. This is what Ikrimah said.

The second: that mercy calls him to lighten the blows so that they do not hurt. This is what Qatadah said.

Al-Junayd derived this meaning, saying: compassion toward the opponents is like turning away from those who fall into sin.

﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ — by punishment is meant the prescribed penalty, which a group of believers witnesses at its carrying out, so that they may be an added deterrent to him and an evidence of the establishment of his punishment. The number of them was disputed, with four opinions:

The first: four or more. This is what Malik and al-Shafi'i said.

The second: three or more. This is what al-Zuhri said.

The third: two or more. Ikrimah said this.

The fourth: one or more. This is what al-Hasan and Ibrahim said.

When God stipulated the faith of those who witness their punishment, some of the scholars of insights said: only one who does not deserve discipline witnesses the places of discipline.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 24, verse 3:

His saying: ﴿The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress or an idolatress﴾, to the end of the verse.

In it there are five aspects.

(p-73) The first: it was revealed specifically concerning a man among the Muslims who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission regarding a woman called Umm Mahzul, who was among the prostitutes of the Jahiliyyah, one of those who raised banners (dhawat al-rayat, i.e. who advertised their trade). She stipulated that he would spend on him, so Allah revealed this verse concerning him and her. This was said by Abdullah ibn Amr and Mujahid.

The second: it was revealed concerning the People of the Suffah (ahl al-Suffah, the poor companions who lodged in the veranda of the mosque). They were a group of the Emigrants (muhajirun), poor, who had no dwellings or tribes in Medina, so they settled in the Suffah of the mosque. They were about four hundred men who sought provision by day and sheltered in the Suffah by night. In Medina there were prostitutes who openly flaunted immorality and who provided men with clothing and food. The People of the Suffah resolved to marry them so that they might have homes and enjoy their food and clothing, and so this verse was revealed concerning them. This was said by Abu Salih.

The third: its meaning is that the fornicator does not commit fornication except with a fornicatress, and the fornicatress is not committed with except by a fornicator. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: it is general in prohibiting the marriage of a fornicatress to a chaste man and the marriage of a chaste woman to a fornicator, and then it was abrogated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa: 3]. This was said by Ibn al-Musayyab.

The fifth: it is specific to the fornicator who has been subjected to the prescribed punishment (mahdud): he does not marry except a fornicatress who has been subjected to the prescribed punishment, and does not marry a woman who has not been so punished, nor a chaste woman. And the fornicatress who has been subjected to the prescribed punishment is not married except by a fornicator who has been so punished, and is not married by one who has not been so punished, nor by a chaste man. This was said by al-Hasan, and Abu Hurayrah narrated it as a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

(p-74) ﴿And that is forbidden to the believers﴾. In it there are two aspects:

One of them: fornication (al-zina).

The second: marriage to fornicators (nikah al-zawani).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 24, verse 4–5:

His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ means: with adultery.

﴿Then they do not bring four witnesses﴾ means: with evidence of the adultery.

﴿Flog them with eighty lashes﴾ This is a hadd (prescribed punishment) that Allah has made obligatory upon the slanderer (qadhif) for the one slandered (maqdhufah). It becomes obligatory upon her demand and falls away with her pardon. Concerning it there are three opinions:

The first: that it is among the rights of human beings, since it becomes obligatory upon demand and falls away with pardon. This is the position of al-Shafi'i.

The second: that it is among the rights of Allah, since it does not transfer to wealth. This is the position of Abu Hanifa.

The third: that it is among the shared rights, combining the right of Allah and the right of human beings, because the two rights are intermingled. This is the position of some later scholars.

The hadd for slander is not complete after puberty and sanity unless both the slanderer and the slandered are free, the slandered is a Muslim, and chaste. If the slandered is a disbeliever or a slave, the slanderer is disciplined (ta'zir) and is not subjected to the hadd. If the slanderer is a disbeliever, he is subjected to the full hadd; and if he is a slave, he is subjected to half the hadd.

﴿And never accept their testimony, and those are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)﴾ This is among the things with which Allah has made slander severe, such that three rulings attach to it: the obligation of the hadd, the designation as a sinner (tafsiq), and the loss of acceptability of testimony.

He did not prescribe a hadd for slander other than adultery, because slander with adultery extends the disgrace (al-ma'arrah) beyond the person to the family and the offspring.

His saying: ﴿Except those who repent after that and make amends﴾ (the verse).

Repentance from slander removes the sin of defiant disobedience (fisq) but does not remove the hadd.

They differed concerning the acceptance of testimony, on four opinions:

The first: his testimony is accepted both before the hadd and after it, since his fisq has been lifted and he has returned to his justice ('adalah). This is the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i, and the majority of the exegetes (jumhur al-mufassirin) said likewise.

The second: his testimony is never accepted, neither before the hadd nor after it. This is the position of Shurayh.

The third: his testimony is accepted by repentance before the hadd, and is not accepted after it. This is the position of Abu Hanifa.

The fourth: his testimony is accepted after the hadd, and is not accepted before it. This is the position of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. al-Sha'bi said: his repentance is accepted, but his testimony is not accepted.

Concerning the manner of repentance there are two opinions:

One of them: that it is by his retracting his own accusation (ikdhab nafsihi). al-Zuhri narrated from Ibn al-Musayyib that Umar ibn al-Khattab flogged Abu Bakrah, Shibl ibn Ma'bad, and Nafi' ibn al-Harith ibn Kaladah, and said to them: "Whoever retracts himself, I will preserve his testimony." Shibl and Nafi' retracted, and Abu Bakrah refused to do so. al-Zuhri said: "By Allah, this is the Sunnah, so preserve it."

The second: that his repentance from it is by the rectification of his condition, his remorse over his slander, seeking forgiveness for it, and abandoning returning to the like of it. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

(p. 76) His saying: ﴿And those who accuse their wives, and have no witnesses except themselves﴾ means: with adultery.

﴿And have no witnesses﴾ means: they testify to the adultery only by themselves. This is a ruling that Allah specified for husbands who accuse their wives, so that they may invoke curses (li'an, mutual oath-imprecation) and the punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf) is removed from them.

Regarding the cause of this, there are two views:

The first: what ʿIkrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Hilal ibn Umayya came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was sitting with his companions and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I came to my family at night and found a man with my family. I saw with my own eyes and heard with my own ears.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked what he had brought and it weighed heavily upon him, until Allah revealed this verse concerning it."

The second: what al-Awzaʿi narrated from al-Zuhri, from Sahl ibn Saʿd: "ʿUwaymir came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, a man found a man with his wife. Should he kill him, and you kill him? Or how should he act?' So Allah revealed this verse. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: '(Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has revealed the Qur'an concerning you and your companion.)' Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded her to invoke curses (mulaʿanah), and she did so with him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: '(Look: if she gives birth to a child with dark skin, wide-set eyes, large buttocks, and thick calves, then I do not think ʿUwaymir is anything but truthful about her. And if she gives birth to one reddish-colored, like a lizard, then I do not think him anything but a liar.)' She then gave birth to him in the description which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had described, confirming ʿUwaymir's truthfulness. (p. 77) Afterwards he was attributed to his mother.'" Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: "He became a governor in Egypt, and he was attributed to a non-father."

If a man accuses his wife of adultery, he has the right to invoke curses (li'an) against her if he wishes, and this right does not belong to any other accuser, because the husband needs to invoke it to deny a lineage that is not his and to lift a bed that has been defiled, which no one else needs. When he wishes to do so, a judge whose ruling is enforceable shall make them invoke curses against each other in the congregational mosque, on the pulpit or in his presence. He begins with the husband while she is present, and he says: "I bear witness by Allah that I am truthful in what I have accused this wife of mine of, of adultery with so-and-so," if he mentions the name in his accusation. If he does not mention it in his invocation, his invocation is still valid.

If he wishes to deny her child, he says: "This child is from adultery, and is not from me." When he has completed what we have described, he repeats it four times, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah that he is surely of the truthful﴾. The "testimony" here is an oath, expressed by the word "testimony," according to the view of Malik and al-Shafiʿi. Abu Hanifa said: it is a testimony, and for this reason the invocation of a disbeliever or a slave is rejected; if it were a testimony, it would not be valid for him to testify on his own behalf and by his own curse. The Arabs call swearing by Allah the Exalted a testimony, as Qays ibn al-Mulawwah said:

"I call Allah to witness that I love her; so this is hers with me, but what is hers with me is nothing for her."

That is, I swear by Allah concerning what I have described of her of adultery. This is the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And the fifth [testimony] that the curse of Allah be upon him if he is among the liars﴾. When he completes the fifth, he has completed his invocation. Then she invokes curses after him, on the pulpit or in his presence, and she says while he is present: "I bear witness by Allah that my husband, this man, is among the liars concerning what he has accused me of of adultery, and that this [child]—if the husband has denied his child from her in his invocation—is not from adultery." She says this four times, and this is the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and it averts from her the punishment﴾, meaning: it repels. Regarding this punishment there are two views:

The first: that it is the hadd (prescribed penalty), which is the position of Malik and al-Shafiʿi.

The second: that it is imprisonment, which is the position of Abu Hanifa.

﴿That she testify four testimonies by Allah that he is surely of the liars﴾. Then she says in the fifth: "And that the wrath of Allah be upon me if he is among the truthful concerning what he has accused me of of adultery." This is the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:

﴿And the fifth that the wrath of Allah be upon her if he is among the truthful﴾. The wrath in her invocation replaces the curse in her husband's invocation. When the mutual invocation is complete, an everlasting separation occurs between them. By what does it take effect? On this there are four opinions:

The first: by the invocation of the husband alone, which is the position of al-Shafiʿi.

The second: by both of their invocations together, which is the position of Malik.

The third: by both of their invocations and the separation by the judge between them, which is the position of Abu Hanifa.

The fourth: by the divorce that the husband pronounces after the invocation, which is the position of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and then she becomes forbidden to him forever.

They differed regarding her being lawful to him again if he retracts his own accusation after the invocation, on two views:

The first: she becomes lawful, which is the position of Abu Hanifa.

The second: she does not become lawful, which is the position of Malik and al-Shafiʿi.

If the husband denies the child by the invocation, the child is attributed to the mother alone and not to him. If he retracts his denial, the child is attributed to him, alive or dead. Abu Hanifa attributed it to him while alive, but not after death.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾. Regarding the bounty of Allah and His mercy here there are two views:

The first: that the bounty of Allah is Islam and His mercy is the Qur'an, said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The second: that the bounty of Allah is from Him, and His mercy is His favor, said by al-Suddi.

The first: its implied meaning is: "Were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy by granting you respite until you repent, you would have been destroyed."

The second: its implied meaning is: "Were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy toward you, there would have befallen the liar among you a great punishment."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 24, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who brought the slander are a band among you﴾. Regarding al-ifk (the slander) there are two views:

The first: that it means sin (ithm). This was said by Abu 'Ubayda.

The second: that it means lying (kadhib).

The poet said:

؎ A witness to the slander, not to the truth, and the witness of the slander is not like al-Ahnaf

﴿A band among you﴾: they were the leaders of the slander: Hassan ibn Thabit, Mistah ibn Uthatha, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Zayd ibn Rifa'a, and Hamnah bint Jahsh. The cause of the slander was that "'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the expedition of al-Muraysi', which is the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, in the sixth year. A necklace of hers made of onyx (jaz' atfar) was lost, and she had gone to attend to her need and then returned to look for it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ departed from his dwelling and her howdah was lifted, and he did not notice that she was not in it, because of her lightness. She returned and found no one in the camp. Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal caught up with her, carried her on his mount, and brought her to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Some people spoke about her and about Safwan. She arrived at Medina, and the slander spread while she did not know of it. Then she learned of it, and something great overwhelmed her, until Allah revealed her innocence thirty-seven days after arriving in Medina, with this verse."

And ﴿Do not think it to be bad for you; rather, it is good for you﴾: that is, do not think that what was mentioned of the slander is bad for you; rather, it is good for you, because Allah has cleared her of it and made its falsity manifest.

Regarding the intended referent of this statement there are two views:

The first: that what is meant is 'A'isha and Safwan, because they were the targets of the slander. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

The second: that what is meant is the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr, and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them both. This was said by Ibn Shajara.

﴿For every man among them is what he has earned of sin﴾: that is, for him is the punishment of what he earned of sin, in proportion to his sin.

﴿And he who took upon himself the greater part of it among them﴾ and the rest of the verse. It was read with a kasra and with a damma on the kaf (kibrahu / kubrahu). Regarding the difference between them there are two views:

The first: that kubrahu with a damma means its greater part, and with a kasra means its sinfulness.

The second: that with a damma it is used for lineage, and with a kasra for the self.

Regarding the one who took upon himself its greater part there are two views:

The first: that he is 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, and the great punishment is Hell. This is the view of 'A'isha, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, and Ibn al-Musayyab.

The second: that he is Mistah ibn Uthatha, and the great punishment is the loss of his sight in this world. This was reported by Yahya ibn Sallam.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Why, when you heard it﴾ means: "Why did you not, when you heard the slander (al-ifk)?"

﴿When the believing men and believing women thought well of their own kind﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: some of them thought well of others, just as they think well of themselves.

The second: they thought of ʿĀ'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) as chaste, just as they thought of themselves.

﴿This is a clear lie (ifk mubin)﴾ means: a manifest falsehood.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it?﴾ means: "Why did they not bring it, if they were truthful, upon it?"

﴿Four witnesses﴾ who testify to what they said.

﴿Since they did not bring the witnesses﴾ — the verse.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 24, verses 20–21:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾ has four interpretations:

First: The sins (khataya) of Satan. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

Second: His traces (athar). This was said by Ibn Shajara.

Third: It is Satan's transgressing from the permissible (halal) to the forbidden (haram), and from obedience (ta'a) to disobedience (ma'siya). This was said by Ibn Isa.

Fourth: It is vows made in acts of disobedience. This was said by Abu Mijlaz.

And it may admit a fifth: that the footsteps of Satan are the transition from one act of disobedience to another, derived from moving the foot by a step (khatw) from one place to another.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And let not those of virtue and wealth among you swear not to give﴾. It was also read as "wa-la yata'alla" (and let him not swear). Regarding the difference between the two readings, there are two aspects.

The first: their meanings are close and one. In this there are two views:

The first: i.e., "let him not fall short," derived from their saying "la alawtu," meaning "I did not fall short." This was stated by Ibn Bahr.

The second: "let him not swear," derived from al-alIyya (ليَّة), which is the oath.

The second view: their meanings differ. So "ya'tali" means "ya'lu" (he falls short) or "yuqsir" (he refrains), and "yata'alla" means "yahlifu" (he swears).

﴿That they should not give to the near of kin, the needy, and those who migrated in the way of Allah﴾, i.e., let them not swear that they will not do good to these people. This verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, who used to spend on Mistah ibn Uthathah. When he engaged in the slander and spread it, Abu Bakr swore that he would not do good to him, and he was his maternal cousin. So Allah forbade him from that oath and urged him to show kindness to him despite his wrongdoing.

This is the meaning of "la ya'lu juhdan" (he spares no effort). What is prohibited in it is refraining from doing good to one who has done wrong, and that we should meet him with kindness and forbearance. So He said: ﴿And let them pardon and overlook﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: that pardon is for deeds and overlooking is for words.

The second: that pardon is concealing the sin without taking it to account, and overlooking is ignoring what is disliked.

﴿Do you not love that Allah should forgive you?﴾, i.e., just as you love that Allah forgive you your sins, so forgive those who wronged you. When Abu Bakr heard this he said: "Yes, O Lord," returned to his kindness, and expiated his oath.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 24, verse 26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women; good women are for good men, and good men are for good women﴾ — the verse.

On it there are three opinions:

The first: wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women; good women are for good men, and good men are for good women. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: wicked deeds are for wicked people, and wicked people are for wicked deeds; good deeds are for good people, and good people are for good deeds. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: wicked words are for wicked people, and wicked people are for wicked words; good words are for good people, and good people are for good words. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak.

Some of the authors of the Khawatir (mystical insights) interpreted it as: the wicked things are the worldly life, and the good things are the Hereafter.

﴿Those are innocent of what they say﴾ — on it there are three opinions:

The first: that ʿĀʾishah and Safwan are innocent of the slander mentioned concerning them. This was said by al-Farra'.

The second: that the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) are innocent of immoralities. This was said by Ibn ʿIsa.

The third: that the good men and good women are innocent of the wicked men and wicked women. This was said by Ibn Shajarah.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿لا تَدْخُلُوا بُيُوتًا غَيْرَ بُيُوتِكم حَتّى تَسْتَأْنِسُوا﴾ فِيهِ ثَلاثَةُ أقاوِيلَ:

أحَدُها: حَتّى تَسْتَأْذِنُوا.

واخْتَلَفَ مَن قالَ بِهَذا التَّأْوِيلِ فَقالَ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ: أخْطَأ الكاتِبُ فِيهِ فَكَتَبَ تَسْتَأْنِسُوا وكانَ يَقْرَأُ: حَتّى تَسْتَأْذِنُوا.

وَقالَ غَيْرُهُ: لِأنَّ (p-٨٦) الِاسْتِئْذانَ مُؤْنِسٌ فَعَبَّرَ عَنْهُ بِالِاسْتِئْناسِ، ولَيْسَ فِيهِ خَطَأٌ مِن كاتِبٍ ولا قارِئٍ.

الثّالِثُ: أنْ تَسْتَأْنِسُوا يَعْنِي أنْ تَعْلَمُوا فِيها أحَدًا اسْتَأْذِنُوهُ فَتُسَلِّمُوا عَلَيْهِ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿فَإنْ آنَسْتُمْ مِنهم رُشْدًا﴾ [النِّساءِ: ٦] أيْ عَلِمْتُمْ، قالَهُ ابْنُ قُتَيْبَةَ.

وَقالَ ابْنُ الأعْرابِيِّ: الِاسْتِئْناسُ الِاسْتِثْمارُ، والإيناسُ اليَقِينُ.

والإذْنُ يَكُونُ بِالقَوْلِ والإشارَةِ.

فَإنْ جاهَرَ فَسُؤالٌ، فَقَدْ رَوى قَتادَةُ عَنْ أبِي هُرَيْرَةَ قالَ: قالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ (ﷺ): «رَسُولُ الرَّجُلِ إذْنُهُ، فَإنِ اسْتَأذَنَ ثَلاثًا ولَمْ يُؤْذَنْ لَهُ ولّى فَلَمْ يُراجِعْ فِي الِاسْتِئْذانِ». وَرَوى الحَسَنُ البَصْرِيُّ «أنَّ [أبا مُوسى] الأشْعَرِيَّ اسْتَأْذَنَ عَلى عُمَرَ (رضي الله عنه) ثَلاثًا فَلَمْ يُؤْذَنْ لَهُ فَرَجَعَ، فَأرْسَلَ إلَيْهِ عُمَرُ فَقالَ: ما رَدَّكَ؟ فَقالَ: قالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ (ﷺ): (مَنِ اسْتَأذَنَ ثَلاثًا فَلَمْ يُؤْذَنْ لَهُ فَلْيَرْجِعْ). فَقالَ عُمَرُ: لِتَجِيئَنِّي عَلى بَيِّنَةٍ أوْ لِأجْعَلَنَّكَ نَكالًا، فَأتى طَلْحَةَ فَشَهِدَ لَهُ». قالَ الحَسَنُ: الأُولى إذْنٌ، والثّانِيَةُ مُؤامَرَةٌ، والثّالِثَةُ عَزْمَةٌ، إنْ شاءُوا أذِنُوا وإنْ شاءُوا رَدُّوا.

وَلا يَسْتَأْذِنُ وهو مُسْتَقْبِلٌ البابَ إنْ كانَ مَفْتُوحًا، وإنْ أُذِنَ لِأوَّلِ القَوْمِ فَقَدْ أُذِنَ (p-٨٧) لِآخِرِهِمْ، ولا يَقْعُدُوا عَلى البابِ بَعْدَ الرَّدِّ فَإنَّ لِلنّاسِ حاجاتٍ.

وَفِي السَّلامِ قَوْلانِ:

الثّانِي: مَسْنُونٌ قَبْلَ الإذْنِ، وإنْ تَأخَّرَ في التِّلاوَةِ فَهو مُقَدَّمٌ في الحُكْمِ، وتَقْدِيرُ الكَلامِ: حَتّى تُسَلِّمُوا وتَسْتَأْذِنُوا، لِما رَوى مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ سِيرِينَ «أنَّ رَجُلًا اسْتَأْذَنَ عَلى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ (ﷺ) فَقالَ: أأدْخُلُ؟ فَقالَ النَّبِيُّ (ﷺ) لِرَجُلٍ عِنْدَهُ: (قُمْ فَعَلِّمْ هَذا كَيْفَ يَسْتَأْذِنُ، فَإنَّهُ لَمْ يُحْسِنْ) فَسَمِعَها الرَّجُلُ فَسَلَّمَ واسْتَأْذَنَ».

وَأوْلى مِن إطْلاقِ هَذَيْنِ القَوْلَيْنِ أنْ يَنْظُرَ: فَإنْ وقَعَتِ العَيْنُ عَلى العَيْنِ قَبْلَ الإذْنِ فَالأوْلى تَقْدِيمُ السَّلامِ، وإنْ لَمْ تَقَعِ العَيْنُ عَلى العَيْنِ قَبْلَ الإذْنِ فَالأوْلى تَقْدِيمُ الِاسْتِئْذانِ عَلى السَّلامِ.

فَأمّا الِاسْتِئْذانُ عَلى مَنازِلِ الأهْلِ: فَإنْ كانُوا غَيْرَ ذِي مَحارِمَ لَزِمَ الِاسْتِئْذانُ عَلَيْهِمْ كالأجانِبِ، وإنْ كانُوا ذَوِي مَحارِمَ وكانَ المَنزِلُ مُشْتَرَكًا هو فِيهِ وهم ساكِنُونَ، لَزِمَ في دُخُولِهِ إنْذارُهُمْ، إمّا بِوَطْءٍ، أوْ نَحْنَحَةٍ مُفْهِمَةٍ، إلّا الزَّوْجَةَ فَلا يَلْزَمُ ذَلِكَ في حَقِّها بِحالٍ، لِارْتِفاعِ العَوْرَةِ بَيْنَهُما.

وَإنْ لَمْ يَكُنِ المَنزِلُ مُشْتَرَكًا فَفِي الِاسْتِئْذانِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَجْهانِ:

أحَدُهُما: أنَّها النَّحْنَحَةُ والحَرَكَةُ.

الثّانِي: القَوْلُ كالأجانِبِ.

وَرَوى صَفْوانُ عَنْ عَطاءِ بْنِ يَسارٍ «أنَّ رَجُلًا قالَ لِلنَّبِيِّ (ﷺ): (أسْتَأْذِنُ عَلى أُمِّي؟) فَقالَ: (نَعَمْ). فَقالَ: إنِّي أخْدُمُها. فَقالَ: (اسْتَأْذِنْ عَلَيْها). فَعاوَدَهُ ثَلاثًا، فَقالَ: (أتُحِبُّ أنْ تَراها عُرْيانَةً؟) قالَ: لا. قالَ: (فاسْتَأْذِنْ عَلَيْها)».

الرّابِعُ: أنَّها الخَراباتُ العاطِلاتُ، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ.

الخامِسُ: أنَّها بُيُوتُ مَكَّةَ، ويُشْبِهُ أنْ يَكُونَ قَوْلَ مالِكٍ.

وَأوْلى مِن إطْلاقِ هَذَيْنِ القَوْلَيْنِ أنْ يَنْظُرَ: فَإنْ وقَعَتِ العَيْنُ عَلى العَيْنِ قَبْلَ الإذْنِ فَالأوْلى تَقْدِيمُ السَّلامِ، وإنْ لَمْ تَقَعِ العَيْنُ عَلى العَيْنِ قَبْلَ الإذْنِ فَالأوْلى تَقْدِيمُ الِاسْتِئْذانِ عَلى السَّلامِ.

أحَدُها: أنَّها الخاناتُ المُشْتَرَكَةُ ذَواتُ البُيُوتِ المَسْكُونَةِ، قالَهُ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ الحَنَفِيَّةِ (رضي الله عنه).

الثّانِي: أنَّها حَوانِيتُ التُّجّارِ، قالَهُ الشَّعْبِيُّ.

الثّالِثُ: أنَّها مُنازِلُ الأسْفارِ ومُناخاتُ الرِّجالِ الَّتِي يَرْتَفِقُ بِها مارَّةُ الطَّرِيقِ في أسْفارِهِمْ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ.

الرّابِعُ: أنَّها الخَراباتُ العاطِلاتُ، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ.

الخامِسُ: أنَّها بُيُوتُ مَكَّةَ، ويُشْبِهُ أنْ يَكُونَ قَوْلَ مالِكٍ.

﴿فِيها مَتاعٌ لَكُمْ﴾ فِيهِ ثَلاثَةُ أقاوِيلَ:

أحَدُها: أنَّها عُرُوضُ الأمْوالِ الَّتِي هِيَ مَتاعُ التُّجّارِ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ.

الثّانِي: أنَّها الخَلاءُ والبَوْلُ، سُمِّيَ مَتاعًا لِأنَّهُ إمْتاعٌ لَهُمْ، قالَهُ عَطاءٌ.

الثّالِثُ: أنَّهُ المَنافِعُ كُلُّها، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ، فَلا يَلْزَمُ الِاسْتِئْذانُ في هَذِهِ المَنازِلِ (p-٨٩) كُلِّها.

قالَ الشَّعْبِيُّ: حَوانِيتُ التُّجّارِ إذْنُهم أنَّهم جاءُوا بِبُيُوتِهِمْ فَجَعَلُوها فِيها وقالُوا لِلنّاسِ: هَلُمَّ.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 24, verse 30:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾. Regarding ﴿min﴾ (from) in this place there are three opinions:

The first: it is a connecting and superfluous particle, and the sense of the sentence is: "Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze." This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: it is used with an implied complement, and its implied sense is: they should lower their gaze from what is not lawful to look at. This is the opinion of Qatada.

The third: it is used in its apparent sense, because lowering the gaze from what is lawful is not required; what is required is lowering it from what is unlawful. Therefore the partitive particle entered upon the lowering of the gaze, so He said: ﴿from their gaze﴾. This was said by Ibn Shajara.

It is forbidden to look at what is intended (with desire), and the first glance that occurs inadvertently is not forbidden.

Al-Hasan al-Basri narrated, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Son of Adam, the first glance is yours, and the second is against you."

﴿and guard their private parts﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: it means by guarding the private parts their chastity, and chastity is (kept) from what is unlawful, not from what is permissible; for this reason the partitive particle did not enter upon it as it entered upon lowering the gaze.

The second: this was said by Abu al-Aliya al-Riyahi. The meaning of guarding the private parts in this place is covering them from sight so that they are not seen. Every place in the Qur'an in which the word "farj" (private part) is mentioned means fornication, except in this place, where the intended meaning is covering. They are called "furuj" (private parts) because they are the openings of the bodily cavities and the passages of what exits from them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 24, verse 31:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment﴾. Zinah (adornment) is what a woman puts on her body so that it beautifies her and makes her pleasing in the eyes, such as jewelry, clothing, kohl and henna. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Take your adornment at every place of worship﴾. The poet said:

"She takes the finest of their adornment that can be seen, and when they go without it, they are not unadorned."

Adornment is of two kinds: apparent and concealed. The apparent adornment does not have to be covered, and it is not forbidden to look at it, based on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except what appears thereof﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions:

(p-91) The first: it is the clothing; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: the kohl and the ring; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Miswar ibn Makhramah.

The third: the face and the two hands; this was said by al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata'.

As for the concealed adornment, Ibn Mas'ud said: the earring, the necklace, the armlet and the anklet. There is disagreement regarding the bracelet. It was narrated from 'A'ishah that it is from the apparent adornment, while others said it is from the concealed adornment, and this is more likely, since it extends beyond the two hands. As for henna, if it is on the two hands, it is from the apparent adornment, and if it is on the two feet, it is from the concealed adornment. This concealed adornment must be covered from non-related men, and it is forbidden for her to deliberately look at it. As for the close relatives (dhu al-mahram), the husband among them is permitted to look and to derive pleasure, while for others, such as fathers, sons and brothers, it is permitted for them to look but forbidden for them to derive pleasure.

Al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, [that they] used to enter upon their sister Umm Kulthum while she was combing her hair.

Some of the authors of the insights (ashab al-khawatir) interpreted this adornment in two ways:

The first: it is this worldly life, so one should not show off what one has been given of it, nor boast except of what appears and is not hidden.

The second: it is the act of obedience, one should not openly display it out of showing off, except what appears and is not concealed. Both of these are far-fetched.

(p-92) ﴿And let them draw their head-coverings over their chests﴾. Khumur are the veils. They were commanded to throw them over their chests to cover their necklines, for they used to throw them over their backs, leaving their necklines exposed. It was also said: their shirts had open collars like a dir'ah (a shift), so their chests showed, and they were commanded to throw the khimar over them to cover them.

The chests are referred to by "collars" because the garment is worn over them.

Then He said: ﴿And not to reveal their adornment except to their husbands﴾. He means that the concealed adornment, its display to the husband, is a solicitation of his inclination and an arousing of his desire. For this reason, "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed the saltā' and the marhā'." The saltā' is the one who does not dye her hands and feet with henna, and the marhā' is the one who does not apply kohl, doing this so that the husband's desire turns away from her; so he commanded her to do that in order to solicit his desire. "And he ﷺ cursed the mufshilah and the musawwifah." The musawwifah is the one who, when he calls her to intimacy, says, "I will do it soon," and the mufshilah is the one who, when he calls her, says, "I am menstruating," while she is not menstruating. It was also narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The ghā'isah and the mughawwisah are cursed." The ghā'isah is the one who does not inform her husband of her menstruation until he has intercourse with her, and the mughawwisah is the one who claims she is menstruating so that her husband refrains from having intercourse with her when she is not menstruating.

(p-93) Our companions differed regarding each of the spouses deliberately looking at the private part of the other with pleasure, on two grounds:

The first: it is permitted, just as enjoying the other is permitted, based on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

The second: it is not permitted, because of what was narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Allah curses the one who looks and the one who is looked at."

As for what lies beyond the two private parts of them, it is permitted for each of them to deliberately look at it from the other, and likewise a slave-woman with her master.

﴿Or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands﴾ up to His saying: ﴿or their brothers' sons﴾. All of these are close relatives (dhu mahram) by the causes and lineages mentioned. It is permitted at all times to look at the concealed adornment for them without arousing their desire, and it is permitted to deliberately look without deriving pleasure.

(p-94) What is obligatory upon a free woman is to cover of her body, in the presence of her close relatives, what lies between her navel and her knee. Likewise it is obligatory with all women, or that some of them cover from others, what lies between the navel and the knee, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿or their women﴾. Regarding them there are two views:

The first: they are the Muslim women; it is not permitted for a Muslim woman to uncover her body before a non-Muslim woman; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: it is general for all women.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿or those whom their right hands possess﴾, meaning their male slaves. A free woman may not be permitted her male slave, though a man may be permitted his female slave, because the sexual part is only deserved by its owner, and a free woman's sexual part does not become the property of her slave, whereas a female slave's sexual part is the property of her master.

Our companions differed regarding the prohibition of what is concealed of a free woman's adornment before her slave, on three views:

The first: it is permitted and not forbidden, and her nakedness with him is like her nakedness with her close relatives, from the navel to the knee, because of his being forbidden to her and because God, may He be exalted, exempted him along with the exemption of her close relatives. This is narrated from 'A'ishah and Umm Salamah.

The second: it is forbidden and not permitted, and her nakedness with him is like her nakedness with men and non-related men, which is all of the body except the apparent adornment, the face and the two hands. The proponent of this view interpreted His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or those whom their right hands possess﴾ as referring to female slaves only, not male slaves. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, 'Ata' and Mujahid also interpreted it this way.

The third: it is permitted for him to look at her in a sense of ease, just as a woman in her household clothes may be bare of the forearms, shins and neck, by consideration of custom and habit, and by removing what preceded. This is the view of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas. As for other than her slave, he is like a free man with her; even if he is the slave of her husband or her mother.

(p-95) Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿or male attendants who have no physical desire﴾. In it there are eight views:

The first: it is the child, because he has no desire for women due to his youth; this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is the impotent, because he has no desire for women due to his incapacity; this is the view of 'Ikrimah and al-Sh'bi.

The third: it is the foolish and simpleminded, because he has no desire for women due to his ignorance; this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata'.

The fourth: it is the castrated, due to the loss of his desire; this is a transmitted view.

The fifth: it is the aged old man, due to the loss of his desire; this is the view of Yazid ibn Habib.

The sixth: it is the fool whom women do not desire and whom men are not jealous of; this is the view of Qatadah.

The seventh: it is the one who seeks food and cares only for his stomach; this is the view of Mujahid.

The eighth: it is the follower of a people who serves them for the sake of his stomach's food; he is diverted and not for desire; this is the view of al-Hasan.

Regarding the source from which the word "irbah" (desire) is derived, there are two views:

The first: it is derived from intellect, from the saying "a man is arib" when he is intelligent.

The second: it is derived from "arab," which means need; this was said by Qutrub.

Then I say: Among these interpretations mentioned, regarding the obligation to cover the concealed adornment from them and the permissibility of what appears of it with them as with others: as for the child, if he has not come to know the nakedness of women and has not distinguished anything of their conditions, then there is no nakedness of the woman with him.

[If he is discerning but not yet of age], it becomes obligatory for the woman to cover from him what lies between her navel and her knee. Regarding whether it is obligatory to cover what is beyond that, there are two views:

The first: it is not obligatory, because the pen is not applied to him and obligation is not binding on him.

The second: it is obligatory, as with a man, because he may desire and be desired.

(p-96) Regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or children who have not yet attained knowledge of women's nakedness﴾, there are three views:

The first: because of their lack of desire.

The second: they do not know women's nakedness because they lack discernment.

The third: they are not able to have intercourse with women.

As for the old man, if desire remains in him, he is like the young. If he lacks it, then there are two views:

The first: the concealed adornment is permitted with him, and the nakedness with him is what lies between the navel and the knee.

The second: it is forbidden with him, and his whole body is nakedness with him except the apparent adornment, in continuation of his previous state.

As for the castrated and the eunuch, there are three views among our companions regarding them:

The first: permissibility of the concealed adornment with both of them.

The second: its prohibition for both of them.

The third: its permissibility for the castrated and its prohibition for the eunuch.

The word 'awrah (nakedness) was named so because of the ugliness of its appearing and the lowering of the gaze from it, derived from 'awar al-'ayn (a defect of the eye).

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known﴾. Qatadah said: a woman, when she walked, would strike with her foot so that the jingling of her anklet could be heard, so they were forbidden from that.

(p-97) Their doing that may have two meanings: either they do it out of joy in their adornment and exuberance, or out of exposing themselves to men and display. If it is the second, then the prohibition against it is absolute, and if it is the first, then the prohibition against it is recommended.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 24, verses 32–34**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And marry off the unmarried (al-ayama) among you﴾. It is the plural of *ayyim* (an unmarried person). Regarding *ayyim*, there are two views:

One: It is the woman whose husband has died. This is the view of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan.

The second: It is the one who has no spouse, whether a virgin or previously married. This is the view of the majority.

It is said: a man is *ayyim* if he has no wife, and a woman is *ayyim* if she has no husband.

Among its uses is what was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "he forbade the *ayyimah*," meaning the unmarried woman. The poet said:

"If you marry, I will marry; and if you remain unmarried, I too will remain unmarried, though I am more likely to be a bachelor than you are."

Al-Qasim narrated: "He ordered the killing of the *ayyim*," meaning the snake.

Regarding this address, there are two views:

One: It is an address to the guardians, that they should marry off their unmarried women to suitable husbands when those women ask for it. This is because it is a command that comes in the form of a binding order, and therefore it is directed to the guardian rather than the husband.

The second: It is an address to the husbands, that they should marry the unmarried women when there is need.

Scholars differed on whether this is obligatory. The literalists (Ahl al-Zahir) held it to be obligatory, adhering to the apparent meaning of the imperative. The majority of jurists (fuqaha') held it to be recommended (mustahabb) for one in need, without being obligatory, and disliked for one not in need.

Then He said: ﴿and the righteous among your male and female servants﴾. There are two interpretations concerning this:

One: The meaning of the speech is: "Marry off the unmarried among you, and the righteous among your men, and marry off your female slaves."

The second, which is the more apparent, is that He commanded the marrying off of slaves, both male and female, just as He commanded the marrying off of the unmarried, because the master has the right of guardianship over his male and female slave. If a female slave asks her master to marry her, he is not obligated to do so, because she is already his concubine (firash). If he wishes to marry her off, it is better for him, even if he does not choose to do so in order to gain the slavery of her offspring and to relieve himself of her maintenance.

If the master wishes to marry off a male slave, or the slave requests this from his master, is the one calling for it entitled to compel the refuser in either case? There are two views on this.

﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: If they are poor in need of marriage, Allah will enrich them through it, protecting them from fornication (sifah).

The second: If they are poor in wealth, Allah will enrich them, either through the contentment of the righteous, or through the combining of the two sources of provision.

Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Rawwad narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Seek riches through this verse: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾."

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: He is abundant in giving and knowing of what is beneficial.

(p-99) The second: He is abundant in provision to His creation.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And let those who do not find the means to marry keep themselves chaste﴾. That is, let them abstain. Chastity (*iffah*), in common usage, means refraining from every indecency. Ru'bah said: "He abstains from its secrets after wickedness."

He means: abstaining from fornication with them.

﴿Those who do not find the means to marry﴾: that is, those who are unable to marry while having the need for it, due to poverty, whether regarding the dowry or the maintenance.

﴿Until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾ admits of two meanings:

One: Allah will make them independent of it through having little desire for it.

The second: He will enrich them with lawful wealth with which they may marry.

﴿And those of your slaves who seek a deed of manumission, write it for them if you know any good in them﴾. As for the manumission (*kitab*) sought here, it is the writing of emancipation for a male or female slave in return for a sum of money. When they pay it, they are freed by it. Before that, they were owners of their earnings, so that they could pay for their freedom. If the master and the slave agree to it, it is permissible. If the master invites the slave to it, he cannot compel the slave to accept it.

If the slave asks for it, is the master compelled to grant it, given that the master sees good in him? There are two views:

One: This is the view of Ata' and Dawud: it is obligatory for the master to write the manumission contract (*mukatabah*), and he is compelled to do so if he refuses.

The second: This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and the majority of jurists: it is recommended for him, but he is not compelled. Once the contract of manumission is concluded, it becomes binding on the part of the master, and the *mukatab* (the slave under the contract) has the choice between continuing it and cancelling it.

﴿If you know any good in them﴾: there are five interpretations:

First: The good is the ability to practise a trade and to earn. This was said by Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas.

Second: The good is wealth. This was said by Ata' and Mujahid.

Third: It is religion and trustworthiness. This was said by al-Hasan.

(p-100) Fourth: It is fidelity and truthfulness. This was said by Qatadah and Tawus.

Fifth: It is earning and trustworthiness. This was said by al-Shafi'i.

﴿And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

One: That is, from the wealth of zakat, from the share allotted to slaves (*riqab*), which the *mukatab* is given so that he may be helped in paying what he owes to his master.

It is not disliked for the master to take it, even if he is wealthy. This was said by al-Hasan, Ibrahim and Ibn Zayd.

The second: From the wealth of the master, as assistance to his *mukatab*, just as others assist him from zakat.

Those who held this interpretation differed on whether it is obligatory. Abu Hanifah held that it is recommended and not obligatory. Al-Shafi'i held that it is obligatory, and this was also the view of Umar, Ali and Ibn Abbas.

Those who held that it is obligatory differed on its amount under this interpretation. It is reported from Ali that he specified it as a quarter of the manumission sum. Al-Shafi'i held that it is not specified, and this was also the view of Ibn Abbas.

If the master refuses to give it willingly, the judge rules on it against him by compulsion, and he exercises his own judgement regarding its amount. If the master dies, it is enforced from his estate, and if he becomes bankrupt, it is shared among his creditors.

According to al-Shafi'i and his companions, the *mukatab* remains a slave as long as a single dirham is still owed. If he fails to pay an installment when it falls due, the master has the choice between granting him more time, cancelling the contract and returning him to slavery. The master does not reclaim what he took from him, nor what was given to him from zakat, nor the wealth he earned.

Al-Kalbi said: The occasion of revelation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿write it for them if you know any good in them﴾ (the verse) was that a slave named Subh, belonging to Huwayyib ibn Abd al-Uzza, asked him to write a manumission contract for him, but Huwayyib refused, so Allah revealed this concerning him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, if they desire chastity﴾. "Slave girls" (*fatayat*) means female slaves. *Bigha'* means fornication, and *tahassun* means chastity. It is not permissible for him to compel them, nor is it possible for them to be compelled, whether they desire chastity or not.

Concerning the mention of compulsion here, there are two views:

One: Because compulsion is valid only regarding one who desires chastity. As for one who does not desire chastity, she is already hastening towards fornication and is not being compelled to it.

The second: That it was revealed in response to a specific occasion, so the prohibition came in the form of that occasion, even though it is not a condition. This is what Jabir ibn Abd Allah narrated: "Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul had a slave girl called Musaykah, and he used to compel her to fornicate. She committed fornication in exchange for a cloak, and she gave it to him. He said: 'Go back and commit fornication with another.' She said: 'No, by Allah, I will not go back.' Then she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'My master compels me to prostitution.' So Allah revealed this verse." This was widespread among the practices of the ignorant, seeking children and earnings.

﴿That you may seek the fleeting goods of this life﴾: that is, that you may take their wages for fornication.

﴿And whoever compels them﴾: that is, from among the masters.

﴿Then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: that is, toward the compelled slave girl, not toward the compelling master.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: He is abundant in giving and knowing of what is beneficial.

(p-99) The second: He is abundant in provision to His creation.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And let those who do not find the means to marry keep themselves chaste﴾. That is, let them abstain. Chastity (*iffah*), in common usage, means refraining from every indecency. Ru'bah said: "He abstains from its secrets after wickedness."

He means: abstaining from fornication with them.

﴿Those who do not find the means to marry﴾: that is, those who are unable to marry while having the need for it, due to poverty, whether regarding the dowry or the maintenance.

﴿Until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾ admits of two meanings:

One: Allah will make them independent of it through having little desire for it.

The second: He will enrich them with lawful wealth with which they may marry.

﴿And those of your slaves who seek a deed of manumission, write it for them if you know any good in them﴾. As for the manumission (*kitab*) sought here, it is the writing of emancipation for a male or female slave in return for a sum of money. When they pay it, they are freed by it. Before that, they were owners of their earnings, so that they could pay for their freedom. If the master and the slave agree to it, it is permissible. If the master invites the slave to it, he cannot compel the slave to accept it.

If the slave asks for it, is the master compelled to grant it, given that the master sees good in him? There are two views:

One: This is the view of Ata' and Dawud: it is obligatory for the master to write the manumission contract (*mukatabah*), and he is compelled to do so if he refuses.

The second: This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and the majority of jurists: it is recommended for him, but he is not compelled. Once the contract of manumission is concluded, it becomes binding on the part of the master, and the *mukatab* (the slave under the contract) has the choice between continuing it and cancelling it.

﴿If you know any good in them﴾: there are five interpretations:

First: The good is the ability to practise a trade and to earn. This was said by Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas.

Second: The good is wealth. This was said by Ata' and Mujahid.

Third: It is religion and trustworthiness. This was said by al-Hasan.

(p-100) Fourth: It is fidelity and truthfulness. This was said by Qatadah and Tawus.

Fifth: It is earning and trustworthiness. This was said by al-Shafi'i.

﴿And give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

One: That is, from the wealth of zakat, from the share allotted to slaves (*riqab*), which the *mukatab* is given so that he may be helped in paying what he owes to his master.

It is not disliked for the master to take it, even if he is wealthy. This was said by al-Hasan, Ibrahim and Ibn Zayd.

The second: It is the one who has no spouse, whether a virgin or previously married. This is the view of the majority.

It is said: a man is *ayyim* if he has no wife, and a woman is *ayyim* if she has no husband.

Al-Qasim narrated: "He ordered the killing of the *ayyim*," meaning the snake.

One: It is an address to the guardians, that they should marry off their unmarried women to suitable husbands when those women ask for it. This is because it is a command that comes in the form of a binding order, and therefore it is directed to the guardian rather than the husband.

The second: It is an address to the husbands, that they should marry the unmarried women when there is need.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 24, verse 35:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾, has four interpretations:

(p-102) The first: its meaning is "Allah is the Guide of the heavens and the earth." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Anas.

The second: "Allah is the Manager (mudabbir) of the heavens and the earth." This was said by Mujahid.

The third: "Allah is the Radiance (diya') of the heavens and the earth." This was said by Ubayy.

The fourth: "the One who illuminates (munawwir) the heavens and the earth."

On this view, there are three interpretations of the means by which He illuminated them:

The first: Allah illuminated the heavens with the angels and illuminated the earth with the prophets.

The second: He illuminated the heavens with awe and illuminated the earth with power.

The third: He illuminated them both with their sun, moon and stars. This was said by al-Hasan and Abu al-ʿAliyah.

﴿The likeness of His light﴾ has four interpretations:

The first: the likeness of the light of Allah. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: the likeness of the light of Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn Shajarah.

The third: the likeness of the light of the believer. This was said by Ubayy.

The fourth: the likeness of the light of the Qur'an. This was said by Sufyan.

So whoever said "the likeness of the light of the believer" means in the heart of the believer himself; whoever said "the likeness of the light of Muhammad" means in the heart of the believer; and whoever said "the light of the Qur'an" means in the heart of Muhammad.

As for whoever said "the light of Allah," there are two views:

One: in the heart of Muhammad.

The second: in the heart of the believer.

﴿like a niche within which is a lamp﴾ has five interpretations:

The first: the niche (mishkah) is a recess with no opening, and the lamp (misbah) is the lamp-flame. This was said by Kaʿb al-Ahbar.

The second: the mishkah is the lamp-holder (qindil) and the misbah is the wick. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: the mishkah is the place of the wick in the lamp-holder, which is like a tube, and the misbah is the light. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: the mishkah is the iron to which the lamp-holder is attached, which is called the chain (silsilah), (p-103) and the misbah is the lamp-holder. This is also narrated from Mujahid.

The fifth: the mishkah is the breast of the believer, the misbah is the Qur'an within it, and the glass (zujajah) is his heart. This was said by Ubayy. Al-Kalbi said: "Mishkah is an Ethiopian word that has been Arabicized."

﴿The lamp is in a glass﴾ has two views:

One: meaning that the fire of the lamp is in the glass of the lamp-holder, because it is brighter there. This is the view of most scholars.

The second: the lamp is the Qur'an and faith, and the glass is the heart of the believer. This was said by Ubayy.

﴿a star brilliant﴾. As for "the star" (kawkab), there are two views:

One: that it is specifically Venus (al-Zuhrah). This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: that it is one of the bright stars, without specification. This is the view of most scholars.

As for "brilliant" (durri), there are four readings:

The first: durrī with a dammah on the dal and without hamzah. This is the reading of Nafiʿ, and its interpretation is that it is luminous, resembling a pearl (durr) in its brightness and purity.

The second: with a dammah and hamzah. This is the reading of ʿĀṣim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, and its interpretation is that it is luminous.

The third: with a kasrah on the dal and hamzah. This is the reading of Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisa'i, and its interpretation is that it is repelling (mutadafiʿ), for by repelling it becomes shooting, and thus stronger in its light; it is derived from daraʾa, meaning dafaʿa, yadfaʿu (to push away).

The fourth: with a kasrah and without hamzah. This is the reading of al-Mufaddal ibn ʿAsim, and its interpretation is that it is flowing, like the shooting stars (al-nujum al-darariyy) that flow from the verb darra al-wadi, meaning the valley flowed when it ran.

﴿kindled from a blessed tree﴾ has two views:

(p-104) One: by "the blessed tree" is meant Abraham, and "the glass that is as if it were a brilliant star" is Muhammad (ﷺ). This is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar.

The second: that it is a description of the light of the lamp, which Allah struck as a parable, meaning that the lamp is kindled from the oil of an olive tree.

﴿blessed﴾: regarding its being made blessed, there are two aspects:

One: because Allah blessed the olives of al-Sham, so it is more blessed than others.

The second: because its branch bears fruit from its beginning to its end, and there is no comparable tree except the pomegranate.

The poet said:

"Blessed is the strange dead, as the fresh pomegranate and olive were blessed."

﴿an olive tree neither of the east nor of the west﴾ has seven interpretations:

The first: that it is not from a tree of the east exclusively, nor from a tree of the west exclusively, because what is specific to one of the two directions yields less oil and is weaker; rather, it is a tree between east and west, like al-Sham, for the two strengths are combined in it. This is the saying of Ibn Shajarah, and it is related from ʿIkrimah.

From this is the saying: "There is no good in the matqah and the madhha." The matqah is the bottom of the valley which the sun does not reach, and the madhha is the top of the mountain from which the sun never departs.

The second: that it is neither of the east, shaded from the sun at sunset, nor of the west, shaded from the sun at sunrise; rather, it is exposed to the sun from sunrise until sunset, so its oil is stronger and brighter. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: that it is in the middle of the tree, which the sun does not reach either when it rises or when it sets, and that is brighter for its oil. This was said by ʿAtiyyah.

(p-105) The fourth: that there is none like it among the trees of the east or the trees of the west. This was related by Yahya ibn Salam.

The fifth: that it is not from the trees of this world, which are either eastern or western, but is from the trees of Paradise. This was said by al-Hasan.

The sixth: that it is a believer, neither eastern nor western, meaning it is not a Christian who prays towards the east, nor a Jew who prays towards the west. This was said by Ibn ʿUmar.

The seventh: that faith is neither harsh nor soft, because among the people of the east there is harshness, and among the people of the west there is softness.

﴿its oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it﴾ has four interpretations:

The first: that the clarity of its oil is like the light of fire, even if no fire touches it. This was mentioned by Ibn ʿIsa.

The second: that the heart of the believer almost recognizes the truth before it is made clear to him, because it agrees with it. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The third: that knowledge almost flows from the mouth of the believing scholar before he speaks it.

The fourth: that the signs of prophethood almost bear witness to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before he calls to them.

﴿Light upon light﴾ has six interpretations:

The first: meaning the light of the fire upon the light of the oil upon the light of the glass. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: the light of prophethood upon the light of wisdom. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: the light of the glass upon the light of fear.

The fourth: the light of faith upon the light of action.

The fifth: the light of the believer, so he is a proof of Allah, followed by another believer who is a proof of Allah, until the earth is not empty of them.

The sixth: the light of a prophet from the offspring of a prophet. This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿Allah guides to His light whom He wills﴾ has three interpretations:

The first: Allah guides to His religion whom He wills of His friends. This was said by al-Suddi.

(p-106) The second: Allah guides to the proofs of His guidance whom He wills of the people of His obedience.

The third: Allah guides to His prophethood whom He wills of His servants.

﴿And Allah sets forth parables for the people﴾, the verse.

Regarding what parable this verse struck, there are three interpretations:

The first: that it is a parable Allah struck for the believer regarding the clarity of the truth to him.

The second: that it is a parable Allah struck for obedience to Him, and He named obedience "light" because it passes beyond its place.

The third: what Ibn ʿAbbas related, that the Jews said: "O Muhammad, how does the light of Allah get out beyond the sky?" So Allah struck this as a parable for His light.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on Surah 24, verses 36–38:

His saying, ﴿in houses﴾: concerning these houses there are two opinions.

One: they are the mosques. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Mujahid.

The second: they are all houses. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

﴿Allah has permitted that they be raised﴾ has four meanings.

The first: that they be built. This was said by Mujahid, as in His saying, ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House﴾, meaning, building it.

The second: that they be purified from impurities and sins. This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: that they be exalted. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: that needs be raised in them to Allah.

(p-107) ﴿and His name be mentioned therein﴾: concerning it there are three sayings.

One: His Book is recited in them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: His most beautiful names are mentioned in them. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

The third: His oneness, that there is no god but Him. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Concerning what the mention of "the houses that Allah has permitted to be raised" refers back to, there are two opinions.

One: to what preceded in His saying, ﴿like a niche in which is a lamp... in houses that Allah has permitted﴾.

The second: to what follows it, His saying, ﴿glorifying Him therein﴾. Concerning this glorification there are two opinions.

One: that it is the declaring of Allah's transcendence.

The second: that it is the prayer. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak.

﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾: al-ghuduww is the plural of ghadwah (morning), and al-'asal is the plural of asil, which is the evening.

﴿Men whom neither commerce nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah﴾. al-Kalbi said: the merchants are the traveling importers (*al-julLab*), and the sellers (*al-ba'a*) are the resident ones.

﴿from the remembrance of Allah﴾: concerning it there are two meanings.

One: from remembering Him by His most beautiful names.

The second: from the call to prayer (*adhan*). This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

﴿in which hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾: concerning it there are five meanings.

The first: it means their turning over upon the edge of Hell.

The second: the changing of their states, such that the Fire scorches them, then ripens them and burns them.

The third: that the turning of hearts is their pounding, and the turning of eyes is looking with them toward the directions of terrors.

The fourth: that the turning of hearts is their reaching the throats, and the turning of eyes is their becoming blue (from terror) after being darkened with kohl, and blindness after sight.

(p-108) The fifth: that the disbeliever, after resurrection, has his heart turned from disbelief to faith, and his sight turned from what he used to see as error to seeing it as right guidance.

﴿so that Allah may reward them for the best of what they did﴾. He mentioned the reward for good deeds and did not mention the reward for bad deeds, although they are also recompensed, for two reasons.

One: it is an encouragement, so He restricted mention to the desire (for reward).

The second: it describes a people from whom major sins do not come, so their minor sins are forgiven.

﴿and increase them from His bounty﴾ admits two meanings.

One: what He multiplies for them from a good deed by ten times its like.

The second: what He bestows as a favor without recompense.

﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾ has four meanings.

The first: without recompense, but bestowing it as a favor.

The second: not measured by sufficiency, so that it exceeds it.

The third: not scant and not restricted.

The fourth: not bestowed with obligation.

It has been said: "When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered the building of the Quba mosque. 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah attended and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, has he who builds mosques already succeeded?' He said: '(Yes, O Ibn Rawahah).' He said: 'And he prayed in them standing and sitting?' He said: '(Yes, O Ibn Rawahah).' He said: 'And why should he spend the night for Allah except prostrating?' He said: '(Yes, O Ibn Rawahah).'" [Then he said:] "Refrain from rhymed prose (*sajʿ*), for no servant has been given anything worse than the eloquence of his tongue."

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on Surah 24, verses 43–44:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He drives along clouds﴾ has two meanings:

First: He sends them down little by little, and from this comes *al-bid'ah al-muzjah* (the meager merchandise), because of its scantiness.

Second: He drives it to wherever He wills. From this comes *zajā al-kharāj* (the tax was driven), when it was carried to its people. Al-Nabigha said:

*"I have come to you from my family and my homeland, driving the remnant of a soul that has scarcely any breath left."*

﴿Then He joins them together﴾, meaning He gathers them, then disperses them when they spread out, so that they grow stronger and connect.

(p-113) ﴿Then He makes it into layers﴾, meaning He stacks some of it upon the rest.

﴿And you see the rain come out from its midst﴾. On this there are two views:

First: *al-wadq* here means lightning, which comes out from among the clouds. The poet said:

*"They raised a dust cloud and came out of it, like the emerging of lightning from the gaps of the clouds."*

This is the view of Abu al-Ashhab.

Second: *al-wadq* means the rain that comes out from among the clouds. This is the view of the majority (*al-jumhur*), and from it is the poet's saying:

*"No cloud has poured its rain, nor has any land made its herbs grow."*

﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains of hail in it﴾. On this there are three views:

First: There are mountains of hail in the sky, and He sends down from those mountains whatever He wills, striking with it whom He wills and diverting it from whom He wills.

Second: He sends down from the sky hail that is like mountains.

Third: *al-sama'* (the sky) here means the cloud, so named for its height, and *al-jibal* (the mountains) is also a description of the cloud, named so for its immensity. From it He sends down hail, striking with it whom He wills and diverting it from whom He wills, so that its striking is a punishment and its diversion is a blessing.

﴿The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight﴾. On this there are three views:

First: *ṣawt barqihi* (the sound of its lightning).

Second: *ḍaw' barqihi* (the light of its lightning). This was said by Yahya ibn Salam, and from it is the saying of al-Shammakh:

*"When it raised its brightness, scarcely could anyone with sight see its light."*

Third: *lam'ān barqihi* (the flashing of its lightning). This was said by Qatada, and the sound arises from the flashing, as Imru' al-Qays said:

(p-114) *"Its brightness shines like the lamps of a monk, who has tilted the pure oil with the twisted wick."*

Thus the lightning is a sign of the thickening of the clouds, a warning of the strength of the rain, and a caution against the descent of thunderbolts.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God alternates the night and the day﴾. On this there are three views:

First: He brings the night after the day and brings the day after the night. This is related by Ibn Isa.

Second: He reduces from the night what He adds to the day, and reduces from the day what He adds to the night. This is related by Yahya ibn Salam.

Third: He changes the day with the darkness of the clouds at times and with the light of the sun at other times, and He changes the night with the darkness of the clouds at times and with the light of the moon at other times. This is related by al-Naqqash.

It may also admit a fourth meaning: that He alternates them according to the variation of the good and evil, benefit and harm, that are decreed within them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah created every creature from water﴾, concerning this there are two opinions:
