**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-‘Uyun) on Surah 24, verses 58–60:**

His saying, ﴿Let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission﴾, there are two opinions concerning them:

(p-120) The first: they are the women, who ask permission only at these particular times, while they ask men's permission at all times. This was said by Ibn ‘Umar.

The second: they are the male and female slaves.

Regarding the meaning of "asking permission," there are three opinions:

The first: only the male slave (not the female slave) asks permission to enter upon his master at these three times. This was said by Ibn ‘Umar and Mujahid.

The second: it refers to the female slaves, because the male slave must always ask permission, at these times and at others. This was said by Ibn ‘Abbas.

The third: it is general, applying to both the male and female slave. This was said by Abu ‘Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami.

﴿And those among you who have not reached puberty (al-hulm)﴾ are the young free children. Whoever among them is not yet discerning (mumayyiz, able to distinguish), who cannot describe what he has seen, is not among those required to ask permission. Whoever is discerning, who can describe what he has seen and relate what he has witnessed, is the one meant by the obligation to ask permission.

﴿Three times: before the dawn prayer, and when you put off your clothes at midday, and after the night prayer of ‘Isha'﴾. These three hours are the times of asking permission for those already mentioned, and they are not obliged to ask permission at other times. He mentioned the first time, which is before the dawn prayer, from waking from sleep until the morning prayer. Then he mentioned the second time, saying ﴿and when you put off your clothes﴾, which is the time of seclusion for the midday nap. Then he mentioned the third time, saying ﴿and after the night prayer﴾, meaning the late prayer, which the common people call al-‘Atamah. It was called al-‘Isha' because the darkness of its time dims (yu‘ashshi) the sight.

He specified these three times because they are the times of a man's seclusion with his family, and because during them there may appear, in his privacy, something of his body that he would dislike to be seen. It has been related that "‘Umar ibn al-Khattab was in his house at the time of the midday rest, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to him a boy from the children of the Ansar called Mudlij. He entered upon ‘Umar without permission while he was sleeping. ‘Umar awoke quickly, and part of his body became uncovered. The boy looked at him, and ‘Umar was saddened and said: 'I wish that Allah, in His grace, had forbidden our sons from entering upon us at these hours without our permission.' Then he went to the Prophet ﷺ and found that this verse had been revealed, so he fell down in prostration [in gratitude to Allah]."

(p-121) ﴿Three times of nakedness (‘awrat) for you﴾: meaning these three hours are the times of nakedness. Thus they have become times of nakedness in terms of time, and they take the same status as the nakedness of bodies; therefore they were singled out for permission.

﴿There is no blame upon you or upon them after these times﴾: concerning this there are two views:

The first: meaning there is no blame upon you, O household members, in relaxing your dress at other times.

The second: there is no blame upon you in forbidding them at other times.

Nor is there blame upon the slaves and the children for not asking permission at times other than these.

﴿They go about attending to you, some of you to others﴾: meaning they constantly go about attending to you for your service, so there is no hardship upon them in entering your dwellings. Those who go about (al-tawwafun) are those who frequently enter and leave.

Then He obligated those children who reach puberty to ask permission when they have had wet dreams and attained maturity, because upon reaching maturity they take the status of men. Thus Allah the Exalted said:

﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked permission﴾, meaning the men.

His saying: ﴿And women past child-bearing (al-qawa‘id min al-nisa')﴾. Al-qawa‘id is the plural of qa‘ida, and they are those who have sat down (qa‘adna) through old age from menstruation and pregnancy, who no longer menstruate and no longer bear children.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "Rather, they were named so because after old age, sitting (al-qu‘ud) becomes frequent among them."

Za‘ma‘a said: "They are not desired, so they sit back from being enjoyed." The first view is more likely.

The poet said:

"Even if what is in her belly were among women who had conceived, and even if the qawa‘id were barren."

His saying: ﴿Who do not hope for marriage (nikah)﴾, meaning that because of old age they do not desire men, and men do not desire them.

﴿There is no blame upon them if they lay aside their garments﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: her jilbab, which is the outer garment above her khimar, so she removes it when the rest of her clothing covers her. This was said by Ibn Mas‘ud and Ibn Jubayr.

The second: her khimar and her outer garment. This was said by Jabir ibn Zayd.

(p-122) ﴿Without displaying adornment (tabarruj)﴾. Tabarruj is that a woman reveals of her adornment that which invites looking at her. This is forbidden for the qawa‘id and for other women alike.

He specified the qawa‘id for laying aside the jilbab only because people's desires turn away from them, as long as nothing of their nakedness appears.

Young women who are desirable are prohibited from laying aside the jilbab or the khimar, and they are commanded to wear the thickest of jalabib, lest their garments reveal their shape.

Mujahid related from Ibn ‘Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "For a husband, what is beneath the dir‘ (shirt) is permitted; for a son and a brother, what is above the dir‘ is permitted; and for a non-mahram, there are four garments: a dir‘, a khimar, a jilbab and an izar."

﴿And that they refrain (yasta‘fifna) is better for them﴾, meaning that if the qawa‘id refrain from laying aside their garments and keep to wearing their jalabib, that is better for them than laying them aside, even though the blame has been lifted from them in this matter.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-‘Uyun) on Surah 24, verses 58–60:**

His saying, ﴿Let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission﴾, there are two opinions concerning them:

(p-120) The first: they are the women, who ask permission only at these particular times, while they ask men's permission at all times. This was said by Ibn ‘Umar.

The second: they are the male and female slaves.

Regarding the meaning of "asking permission," there are three opinions:

The first: only the male slave (not the female slave) asks permission to enter upon his master at these three times. This was said by Ibn ‘Umar and Mujahid.

The second: it refers to the female slaves, because the male slave must always ask permission, at these times and at others. This was said by Ibn ‘Abbas.

The third: it is general, applying to both the male and female slave. This was said by Abu ‘Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami.

﴿And those among you who have not reached puberty (al-hulm)﴾ are the young free children. Whoever among them is not yet discerning (mumayyiz, able to distinguish), who cannot describe what he has seen, is not among those required to ask permission. Whoever is discerning, who can describe what he has seen and relate what he has witnessed, is the one meant by the obligation to ask permission.

﴿Three times: before the dawn prayer, and when you put off your clothes at midday, and after the night prayer of ‘Isha'﴾. These three hours are the times of asking permission for those already mentioned, and they are not obliged to ask permission at other times. He mentioned the first time, which is before the dawn prayer, from waking from sleep until the morning prayer. Then he mentioned the second time, saying ﴿and when you put off your clothes﴾, which is the time of seclusion for the midday nap. Then he mentioned the third time, saying ﴿and after the night prayer﴾, meaning the late prayer, which the common people call al-‘Atamah. It was called al-‘Isha' because the darkness of its time dims (yu‘ashshi) the sight.

He specified these three times because they are the times of a man's seclusion with his family, and because during them there may appear, in his privacy, something of his body that he would dislike to be seen. It has been related that "‘Umar ibn al-Khattab was in his house at the time of the midday rest, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to him a boy from the children of the Ansar called Mudlij. He entered upon ‘Umar without permission while he was sleeping. ‘Umar awoke quickly, and part of his body became uncovered. The boy looked at him, and ‘Umar was saddened and said: 'I wish that Allah, in His grace, had forbidden our sons from entering upon us at these hours without our permission.' Then he went to the Prophet ﷺ and found that this verse had been revealed, so he fell down in prostration [in gratitude to Allah]."

(p-121) ﴿Three times of nakedness (‘awrat) for you﴾: meaning these three hours are the times of nakedness. Thus they have become times of nakedness in terms of time, and they take the same status as the nakedness of bodies; therefore they were singled out for permission.

﴿There is no blame upon you or upon them after these times﴾: concerning this there are two views:

The first: meaning there is no blame upon you, O household members, in relaxing your dress at other times.

The second: there is no blame upon you in forbidding them at other times.

Nor is there blame upon the slaves and the children for not asking permission at times other than these.

﴿They go about attending to you, some of you to others﴾: meaning they constantly go about attending to you for your service, so there is no hardship upon them in entering your dwellings. Those who go about (al-tawwafun) are those who frequently enter and leave.

Then He obligated those children who reach puberty to ask permission when they have had wet dreams and attained maturity, because upon reaching maturity they take the status of men. Thus Allah the Exalted said:

﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked permission﴾, meaning the men.

His saying: ﴿And women past child-bearing (al-qawa‘id min al-nisa')﴾. Al-qawa‘id is the plural of qa‘ida, and they are those who have sat down (qa‘adna) through old age from menstruation and pregnancy, who no longer menstruate and no longer bear children.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "Rather, they were named so because after old age, sitting (al-qu‘ud) becomes frequent among them."

Za‘ma‘a said: "They are not desired, so they sit back from being enjoyed." The first view is more likely.

The poet said:

"Even if what is in her belly were among women who had conceived, and even if the qawa‘id were barren."

His saying: ﴿Who do not hope for marriage (nikah)﴾, meaning that because of old age they do not desire men, and men do not desire them.

﴿There is no blame upon them if they lay aside their garments﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: her jilbab, which is the outer garment above her khimar, so she removes it when the rest of her clothing covers her. This was said by Ibn Mas‘ud and Ibn Jubayr.

The second: her khimar and her outer garment. This was said by Jabir ibn Zayd.

(p-122) ﴿Without displaying adornment (tabarruj)﴾. Tabarruj is that a woman reveals of her adornment that which invites looking at her. This is forbidden for the qawa‘id and for other women alike.

He specified the qawa‘id for laying aside the jilbab only because people's desires turn away from them, as long as nothing of their nakedness appears.

Young women who are desirable are prohibited from laying aside the jilbab or the khimar, and they are commanded to wear the thickest of jalabib, lest their garments reveal their shape.

Mujahid related from Ibn ‘Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "For a husband, what is beneath the dir‘ (shirt) is permitted; for a son and a brother, what is above the dir‘ is permitted; and for a non-mahram, there are four garments: a dir‘, a khimar, a jilbab and an izar."

﴿And that they refrain (yasta‘fifna) is better for them﴾, meaning that if the qawa‘id refrain from laying aside their garments and keep to wearing their jalabib, that is better for them than laying them aside, even though the blame has been lifted from them in this matter.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 24, verse 61:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves﴾. Concerning it there are five opinions:

The first: The Ansar used to avoid eating with these people when they were invited to a meal. They would say: "The blind man cannot see the best of the food, the lame man cannot manage the crowding at the meal, and the sick man is too weak to share the food with the healthy." They also used to say: "Their food is separate, and they consider it better than being partners." So God revealed this verse concerning them and lifted the blame from them regarding eating with them. This was related by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi.

The second: There is no blame upon these people among the disabled for eating from the houses of those whom God mentioned after this, from their families. This was related by Mujahid.

The third: The disabled people mentioned used to take the place of the Ansar in their homes when they went out to fight, and they would avoid eating from those homes. So God permitted them to eat from the homes of those whom they had left in charge of them. This was related by al-Zuhri.

The fourth: It was revealed concerning the dropping of jihad for those among the disabled who were mentioned.

The fifth: There is no blame upon those among the disabled who are mentioned, if they are invited to a wedding feast, for them to take their guide with them. This is the saying of 'Abd al-Karim.

﴿Nor upon yourselves that you eat from your houses﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions:

The first: From the property of your dependants and your wives, because they are in your house.

The second: From the houses of your children. He attributed the children's houses to the houses of their fathers, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "You and your wealth belong to your father." For this reason God did not mention the houses of the sons when He mentioned the houses of the fathers and relatives, being content with this mention.

The third: By these are meant the houses in which they live, serving their owners and connected to their masters, such as the household and the servants.

﴿Or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers, or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts﴾. Thus He permitted eating from the houses of these people by virtue of kinship, without seeking their permission to eat, provided the food is available (mabdhul). If it is kept secured away from them, it is not permissible for them to break open its security.

It is not permissible for them to go beyond eating to storing (food), nor to taking what is not food, even if it is not secured from them, except with their permission. Then He said: ﴿Or that whose keys you possess﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions:

The first: By it is meant a man's agent and steward over his estate, who may eat of what he oversees of the produce of the estate. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: It means the man's own dwelling, from which he eats what he has stored. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: By it is meant the master's eating from the dwelling and property of his slave, because the slave's property belongs to his master. This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

﴿Or your friend﴾. Concerning it there are two sayings:

One of them: He may eat from his friend's house at a wedding feast only, and not otherwise.

The other: He may eat from his friend's house at a wedding feast and otherwise, when the food is present and not secured.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The friend is more (than the parents). Do you not see that the people of Hell did not seek help from fathers or mothers, but only said: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor a warm friend﴾." It is also related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God has placed in a righteous friend a substitute for the blameworthy kinship." By "friend" is meant friends, and it is singular used to express the plural. Jarir said:

They called upon desire, then they shot our hearts
With the arrows of enemies, and they are friends.

Concerning "friend" there are two sayings:

One of them: He is the one who is sincere to you in his affection.

The other: He is the one whose inner self agrees with your inner self, just as his outward self agrees with your outward self.

Then they differed concerning the abrogation (naskh) of what was mentioned before, after the establishment of its ruling, into two opinions:

One of them: It remains in force, and nothing of it has been abrogated. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: It is abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless permission is given to you for a meal﴾, and the rest of the verse.

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with his good pleasure."

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿There is no blame upon you that you eat together or separately﴾. Concerning it there are four aspects:

The first: It was revealed concerning the tribe of Kinanah. A man among them considered it forbidden for himself to eat alone in the pre-Islamic period, to the extent that a man would drive a flock of camels, though hungry, until he found someone to eat and drink with him. So God revealed this verse concerning them. This was said by Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: It was revealed concerning a people of the Arabs, among whom a man, when a guest came to him, would avoid leaving him to eat alone until he ate with him. So this was revealed concerning them. This was said by Abu Salih.

The third: It was revealed concerning a people who avoided eating together, believing it to be a sin, and each one of them would eat alone. So this was revealed concerning them. This was related by al-Naqqash.

The fourth: It was revealed concerning travellers who shared their provisions, so that whenever one of them was late, the others would refrain from eating until he arrived. So this was revealed concerning them, as a concession to eat together or separately.

﴿So when you enter houses﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions:

One of them: They are the mosques.

The second: They are all houses.

﴿Then greet one another﴾. Concerning it there are five opinions:

The first: It means, when you enter your own houses, greet your family and dependants. This was said by Jabir.

The second: When you enter the mosques, greet those who are in them. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: When you enter the houses of others, greet them. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: When you enter houses, greet the people of your religion. This was said by al-Suddi.

The fifth: When you enter empty houses, greet yourselves, which is to say: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God." This was said by Ibn 'Umar, Ibrahim and Abu Malik. It was also said: his greeting upon himself is to say: "Peace be upon us from our Lord," as a greeting from God.

If one person from the group greets, it suffices for all of them. When a man enters a mosque with a large gathering, he greets in a way that makes himself hear; and if the gathering is small, he makes them hear, or some of them.

Al-Hasan said: "Women used to greet men, and men did not greet women." Ibn 'Umar used to greet women. Had it been said that neither party greets the other, it would have been better, because greeting is a bond of connection.

﴿A greeting from God﴾. Concerning it there are four opinions:

The first: It means that "peace" (al-salam) is one of the names of God, may He be exalted.

The second: That greeting with peace is one of God's commands.

The third: That the response to the greeting is a supplication for him with God.

The fourth: That the angels respond to him, so it is a reward from God.

﴿Blessed﴾. Concerning it there are two aspects:

One of them: Because of the abundant reward in it.

The second: Because of the reward hoped for in the supplication.

﴿Good﴾ may carry two meanings:

One of them: Because of the good life in it through mutual connection.

The second: Because of the good remembrance and standing in it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when they are with him upon a gathering matter﴾ has three opinions:

The first: the gathering matter is the Friday prayer, the two festivals (al-'Idan), the prayer for rain (al-Istisqa'), and everything at which a sermon (khutbah) is delivered. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

The second: it is jihad. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: it is obedience to Allah. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿They do not depart until they seek his permission﴾, meaning: they do not leave him until they ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to do so.

﴿So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs…﴾ (the verse).

This is according to what he sees of their excuses and their intentions. It is related that this was revealed concerning Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), who "was with the Prophet (ﷺ) on the expedition of Tabuk, and he asked him permission to return to his family, and he said: 'Go, for by Allah, you are neither a hypocrite nor a doubter.'" When the hypocrites asked for permission, he would look at them and not grant it to them, so some of them would say to others: "Muhammad claims that he was sent with justice, and yet this is how he treats us."

﴿And ask Allah's forgiveness for them﴾, meaning for whoever among the believers he granted permission to, so that by his seeking forgiveness the blame of departing would be removed from him. Qatadah said: this verse abrogates (naskh) the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah pardon you; why did you grant them permission?﴾ (the verse).

(p-١٢٨)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 24, verses 63–64:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like the calling of some of you to others﴾, to the end of the verse.

In it there are three opinions:

First: It is a prohibition from Allah against provoking the calling of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by angering him, because his calling entails punishment and is not like the calling of others. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: It is a prohibition from Allah against calling the Messenger of Allah with harshness and rudeness; rather, one should call him with humility and submissiveness, saying: "O Messenger of Allah, O Prophet of Allah." This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

Third: It is a prohibition from Allah against delay when he commands them and against lagging behind when he summons them to jihad; they should not lag behind as some of them lag behind from responding to others. This was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away, sheltering one another﴾. In it there are two opinions:

One: They were the hypocrites, who would slip away from the Friday prayer, "liwadhan" meaning that some of them would cling to others, joining them in concealment from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because nothing was heavier upon the hypocrites than the day of Friday and attending the sermon; so this was revealed concerning them. This was related by al-Naqqash.

Two: They would slip away from jihad, retreating from it, clinging to one another "liwadhan"; so this was revealed concerning them. This was said by Mujahid.

Al-Hasan said that the meaning of His saying ﴿liwadhan﴾ is "fleeing from jihad." From it is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:(p-129)

Quraysh roams about from you, sheltering one another; it has not preserved [its covenant], and its intellects have become light.

﴿So let those who oppose his command beware﴾. In it there are two opinions:

One: They oppose the command of Allah; this was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

Two: They oppose the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); this was said by Qatadah.

The meaning of His saying ﴿oppose his command﴾ is "turn away from his command." Al-Akhfash said: "ʿan" in this place is superfluous, and the meaning of the statement is "let those who oppose his command beware," whether what he commanded them was a matter of religion or of worldly affairs.

﴿Lest a trial afflict them﴾. In it there are three interpretations:

One: disbelief; this was said by al-Suddi.

Two: punishment; this was said by Ibn Kamil.

Three: a calamity that reveals what is in their hearts of hypocrisy; this was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

﴿Or a painful punishment afflict them﴾. In it there are two opinions:

One: killing in this world; this was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

Two: punishment in Hell in the Hereafter.
